paragraphs: Swamiji once described the many ways human beings have loved God. One of the sweetest is Madhura, the love between husband and wife. Saints like St. Teresa loved God this way. Persian mystics pictured God as the beloved wife, while in India God is pictured as the husband. Queen Mira Bai taught that the Divine Spouse was everything, and the story of Krishna and the Gopi girls belongs to this same mood.

Swamiji admitted that this kind of devotion can be misused and can drag people down. But, he asked, would you stop cooking because beggars exist, or own nothing because there are thieves? Many great saints grew through it. Its fruit is a love so free that it no longer needs any sect or ritual; everything becomes love for love's sake.

Beyond even this, he said, is love without any distinction at all, the love of the Self. To show it, he told a Persian poem. A lover came to his beloved's door and knocked. From inside she asked who was there. He gave his name, adding that he was her beloved. She sent him away, saying she knew no such person. He came back again and again. On the fourth time, when she asked, he answered that he was her own self, and the door swung open.

Swamiji also shared the words of a great saint who spoke as a young girl in love: when their eyes met, both souls were changed, until she could no longer tell who was the man and who the woman. Once there had been two; love came, and there was only one.
His conclusion was simple. Every other kind of love fades quickly. In the highest love the union is of spirit alone, and only that lasts and keeps on growing.
learn: Love that depends on looks, moods or what we get from each other tends to fade fast. The love that lasts goes deeper, where the line between 'me' and 'you' starts to blur. That is worth remembering in friendships and relationships, not just in spiritual life.
